questions.question: How does binary search work and what is its time complexity?
questions.title: Binary Search Algorithm Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **Binary search** finds a target in a **sorted array** by repeatedly halving the search range. Compare the target with the **middle element**: if equal you're done, if the target is smaller search the left half, if larger search the right half. Each step throws away half the data, giving **O(log n)** time and **O(1)** space for the iterative version.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can state the sorted-array precondition, write the loop without off-by-one errors, and justify the O(log n) bound
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Computing mid as (left + right) / 2 (overflows for large indices) and updating boundaries to mid instead of mid +/- 1, causing infinite loops
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Say each comparison halves the range, so ~20 steps cover a million elements, and use the overflow-safe mid formula without being asked

sections.title: Binary Search: Halve the Range Every Step
sections.content:
**Binary search** is a **divide-and-conquer** lookup that works only on a **sorted array**. Instead of scanning every element (**linear search**, O(n)), it keeps two pointers, `left` and `right`, that bound the part of the array still worth checking. Each iteration looks at the **middle element** and uses the sorted order to throw away half the remaining range.

Think of finding a word in a dictionary: you open near the middle, decide whether your word is before or after, and repeat on that side. Because every comparison removes half the candidates, the array shrinks 1000 -> 500 -> 250 -> ... and a million elements need only about **20 comparisons**. That is the meaning of **O(log n)**.

The one hard precondition: the array must be **sorted**. Without sorted order, the middle element tells you nothing about which side the target is on, so the elimination step is invalid.

sections.title: Binary Search Control Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[left = 0
right = n-1] --> B{left <= right?} B -- no --> F[return -1
not found] B -- yes --> C[mid = left + right-left/2] C --> D{compare
nums mid vs target} D -- equal --> E[return mid] D -- nums mid < target --> G[left = mid + 1
search right half] D -- nums mid > target --> H[right = mid - 1
search left half] G --> B H --> B ```

sections.title: Linear search - O(n), checks every element
Binary search - O(log n), needs sorted input
Dry Run on a Sorted Array
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Overflowing mid**: `mid = (left + right) / 2` overflows when `left + right` exceeds `Integer.MAX_VALUE`. Use `mid = left + (right - left) / 2`.
- **Wrong boundary move**: setting `left = mid` or `right = mid` (without +/- 1) can loop forever when only two elements remain. Always move past `mid`.
- **Unsorted input**: binary search on unsorted data returns garbage. Sort first, or use a different structure.
- **Wrong loop condition**: `while (left < right)` can miss the last element; the inclusive template uses `left <= right`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Precondition**: the array must be **sorted**, or the halving logic is invalid.
- **Time**: **O(log n)** - each comparison discards half the range.
- **Space**: **O(1)** iterative; **O(log n)** recursive due to the call stack.
- **Overflow-safe mid**: `left + (right - left) / 2`, never `(left + right) / 2`.
- **Inclusive template**: `while (left <= right)`, move boundaries to `mid + 1` / `mid - 1`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Binary search is a divide-and-conquer way to find a value in a sorted array, and it runs in O of log n time. I keep two pointers, left at the start and right at the end of the array. In each step I look at the middle element. If it equals my target, I'm done and I return that index. If the target is smaller than the middle, then because the array is sorted I know it can only be in the left half, so I move right to mid minus one. If the target is larger, it must be in the right half, so I move left to mid plus one. I repeat until I either find the value or the pointers cross, which means it isn't there. The reason this is so fast is that every single comparison throws away half of what's left, so even a million elements only take about twenty comparisons, compared to up to a million for a plain linear scan. Two things I'm always careful about as a fresher. First, I compute the middle as left plus the quantity right minus left divided by two, instead of left plus right divided by two, because adding two large indices can overflow an int and wrap to a negative number. Second, the array genuinely has to be sorted first, otherwise the middle element tells me nothing about which side to keep, and the whole elimination idea breaks down. The iterative version uses constant extra space; the recursive version uses O of log n space for the call stack.

questions.question: What is the difference between Arrays.binarySearch() and a manual binary search in Java?
questions.title: Arrays.binarySearch vs Manual Binary Search Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: **`Arrays.binarySearch()`** is Java's built-in binary search on a pre-sorted array: it returns the index if found, or the encoded value **`-(insertionPoint) - 1`** if not. A **manual binary search** is the loop you write yourself, which you need for variants the library can't do - first/last occurrence, rotated arrays, or binary search on an answer space. Both are O(log n); the difference is control versus convenience.

interviewer_intent.testing: Knowledge that the library exists, what its negative return value means, and when its limits force a manual implementation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating any negative result as plain -1 and missing the encoded insertion point, or forgetting the array must be sorted first
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Decode the insertion point with -(returnValue + 1) and name a concrete variant (first occurrence, rotated search) the library cannot handle

sections.title: Built-in vs Hand-Written Binary Search
sections.content:
Java ships **`Arrays.binarySearch(array, key)`** for binary search over a **sorted** array. On a hit it returns the index. On a miss it does not return `-1`; it returns **`-(insertionPoint) - 1`**, where `insertionPoint` is where the key would go to keep the array sorted. So a miss that belongs at index 3 returns `-4`. Decode it with `insertionPoint = -(returnValue + 1)`.

A **manual binary search** is the `while (left <= right)` loop you write yourself. You reach for it when you need behaviour the library does not offer: the **first or last occurrence** of a duplicated value, search in a **rotated sorted array**, a custom comparison, or **binary search on the answer** (capacity / square-root style problems where there is no array at all).

sections.title: Two Tools, One Algorithm
sections.content:
blue|Arrays.binarySearch|~built-in, sorted input|index if found|-(insertion)-1 if missing|one line, JDK-tested
amber|Manual loop|~you control boundaries|first / last occurrence|rotated-array search|answer-space search
emerald|Shared truth|~both are O(log n)|need monotonic order|halve the range each step|sort before searching

sections.title: Arrays.binarySearch() vs Manual
sections.content:
| Aspect | `Arrays.binarySearch()` | Manual binary search |
|---|---|---|
| Not-found result | `-(insertionPoint) - 1` (encoded) | Whatever you choose, usually `-1` |
| Effort | One line | ~15 lines, easy to introduce bugs |
| Variants (first/last, rotated) | Not supported | Fully supported |
| Answer-space search | No array -> can't use it | Works (capacity, sqrt) |
| Reliability | JDK-tested, optimized | Depends on your code |

Use the library for plain existence/index checks; write your own only when you need a variant.

sections.title: Misreading the library miss as -1
Decoding the insertion point correctly
When to Use Each
sections.content:
- **`Arrays.binarySearch()`**: the array is already sorted and you only need 'is it here / at what index'. Less code, fewer bugs.
- **Manual**: you need the **first/last** occurrence among duplicates, search in a **rotated** array, a **custom Comparator** beyond what the overload supports, or **binary search on an answer space** where there is no physical array.
- **Neither**: the data isn't sorted and you won't keep it sorted - a `HashSet`/`HashMap` lookup at O(1) usually beats sorting just to binary search.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- A miss returns **`-(insertionPoint) - 1`**, not `-1`; decode with `-(r + 1)`.
- The array **must be sorted** first, or results are undefined.
- There is a `Comparator` overload, but it still can't do first/last or rotated variants.
- Prefer the library for simple cases; write your own only for variants.
- Both are **O(log n)** time.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Arrays dot binarySearch is Java's built-in binary search for a sorted array. If the key is present it returns the index. The part freshers trip on is what it returns when the key is absent. It does not return minus one. It returns minus the insertion point minus one, where the insertion point is where the value would go to keep the array sorted. So if a missing value would belong at index two, it returns minus three. You decode the insertion point as minus the quantity return value plus one. That encoding is actually useful, because a single call tells you both that the value is missing and where it should be inserted. A manual binary search is the loop you write by hand, and I reach for it whenever I need something the library can't do. The classic cases are finding the first or last occurrence of a value that appears multiple times, searching in a rotated sorted array, or doing binary search on an answer space, like finding a minimum capacity, where there's no array to pass in at all. So my rule is simple. For a straightforward existence or index check on already-sorted data, I use the library method because it's one line and thoroughly tested. The moment the problem is a variant, I write the loop myself so I control exactly how the boundaries move. And in both cases the array has to be sorted first, and both run in O of log n time.

questions.question: What is the difference between finding the first and last occurrence of an element using binary search?
questions.title: Binary Search First Last Occurrence
questions.direct_answer: Both reuse the binary-search loop but **don't stop on the first match**. For the **first occurrence**, on a match record `mid` and keep searching **left** (`right = mid - 1`). For the **last occurrence**, on a match record `mid` and keep searching **right** (`left = mid + 1`). You store the best index so far and keep narrowing, so both stay **O(log n)**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can adapt the binary-search template to boundary-finding instead of memorizing one version
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Returning immediately on the first match, which gives some occurrence but not the leftmost or rightmost
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Note both variants share one template and differ only in the direction you keep searching after a match

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Record `mid` on a match, then **keep narrowing** instead of returning.
- **First** -> go left (`right = mid - 1`); **Last** -> go right (`left = mid + 1`).
- One template, one differing line - shows pattern understanding.
- Count of a value = `last - first + 1`, all in **O(log n)**.
- Initialize `ans = -1` so a missing target is reported cleanly.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: The only real difference between finding the first and the last occurrence is which direction you keep searching after you hit the target. Standard binary search returns the moment it finds a match, but in a sorted array with duplicates that match could be any of the copies, so I change the loop so it doesn't stop early. For the first occurrence, when the middle element equals the target, I save that index in an answer variable and then move right down to mid minus one. That keeps me searching the left half, because if there's an earlier copy it has to be on the left. I only commit to the answer once the range is exhausted. For the last occurrence it's the mirror image. On a match I save the index and move left up to mid plus one, which keeps me searching the right half for a later copy. The important thing is that both versions are the exact same template, and they differ in just one line, the direction I move after a match. That's what I'd want the interviewer to hear, because it shows I understand the pattern rather than memorizing two separate functions. A common mistake is returning straight away on the first match, which gives you a valid index but not specifically the leftmost or rightmost one. Another is scanning linearly once you find a hit, which collapses to O of n if everything is a duplicate. Done correctly, each search is O of log n, and running both lets me count how many times the value appears as last minus first plus one.

sections.title: Understand the decision
sections.content:
Binary search the **answer space** from 1 to n.

For the integer square root: if `mid*mid == n` return `mid`; if `mid*mid < n` record `mid` and go right (`left = mid + 1`); else go left (`right = mid - 1`).

Both reuse the binary-search loop but **don't stop on the first match**. For the **first occurrence**, on a match record `mid` and keep searching **left** (`right = mid - 1`). For the **last occurrence**, on a match record `mid` and keep searching **right** (`left = mid + 1`). You store the best index so far and keep narrowing, so both stay **O(log n)**.

Computing mid as (left + right) / 2 (overflows for large indices) and updating boundaries to mid instead of mid +/- 1, causing infinite loops

sections.title: First-Occurrence Decision Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[left=0, right=n-1
ans = -1] --> B{left <= right?} B -- no --> Z[return ans] B -- yes --> C[mid = left + right-left/2] C --> D{nums mid vs target} D -- equal --> E[ans = mid
right = mid - 1
keep going LEFT] D -- less --> F[left = mid + 1] D -- greater --> G[right = mid - 1] E --> B F --> B G --> B ```

sections.title: First and Last Occurrence with Dry Run
Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Returning on first match**: `if (nums[mid] == target) return mid;` gives an arbitrary copy, not the boundary.
- **Forgetting to store `mid`**: moving the boundary without saving `ans` loses the match you just found.
- **Mixing directions**: for the *first* occurrence you move *right* down (`right = mid - 1`); freshers often do the opposite.
- **Linear scan after a hit**: walking left/right from a match degrades to O(n) on `{2,2,...,2}`.

sections.content: **`Arrays.binarySearch()`** is Java's built-in binary search on a pre-sorted array: it returns the index if found, or the encoded value **`-(insertionPoint) - 1`** if not. A **manual binary search** is the loop you write yourself, which you need for variants the library can't do - first/last occurrence, rotated arrays, or binary search on an answer space. Both are O(log n); the difference is control versus convenience.

questions.question: Why do you use mid = left + (right - left) / 2 instead of (left + right) / 2 in binary search?
questions.title: Binary Search Mid Calculation Overflow
questions.direct_answer: `left + right` can **overflow** a 32-bit `int` when both are near `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, wrapping to a negative number and producing a garbage `mid`. `left + (right - left) / 2` is mathematically the same midpoint but keeps the intermediate value bounded, because `right - left` is always smaller than either endpoint. Java overflow is **silent** - no exception - so the bug shows up as wrong results.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of silent integer overflow and attention to detail in a 'trivial' line of code
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming Java throws on overflow, or thinking (left + right) / 2 is always fine because it works on small arrays
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: State the exact failure condition - left + right exceeding Integer.MAX_VALUE - and that it matters for answer-space searches up to 2 billion

sections.title: Why the Midpoint Formula Matters
sections.content:
The intuitive midpoint `(left + right) / 2` is mathematically correct but has a hidden trap: **integer overflow**. A Java `int` is 32-bit signed with a maximum of `Integer.MAX_VALUE` = 2,147,483,647. If `left` and `right` are both large - which happens when you **binary search an answer space** up to ~2 billion, not just a normal array - their **sum** exceeds the max. Java does **not** throw; the value silently **wraps to a negative number**, so `mid` becomes negative and you index out of bounds or compute nonsense.

`left + (right - left) / 2` gives the same midpoint but never forms that oversized sum: `right - left` is the size of the current range, always smaller than either endpoint, so it can't overflow. You halve that gap and add it back to `left`.

sections.title: Unsafe vs Safe Midpoint
Overflow at a Glance
sections.content:
rose|The Bug|~int sum wraps silently|left + right > 2.1 billion|wraps to negative mid|no exception thrown
amber|Why It Hides|~works on small inputs|fine for LeetCode-size arrays|fails on answer-space searches|hard to reproduce
emerald|The Fix|~bound the intermediate|right - left is range size|always smaller than endpoints|same midpoint, zero cost

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking Java warns you**: integer overflow is silent - no `ArithmeticException`, just wrong values.
- **'It always works'**: `(left + right) / 2` works until indices get large (answer-space binary search), then fails rarely and mysteriously.
- **Vague explanation**: saying 'it overflows' without naming the cause - two large positive ints summing past `Integer.MAX_VALUE` and wrapping negative.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Failure condition**: `left + right` exceeds `Integer.MAX_VALUE` (~2.1 billion).
- Java overflow is **silent** and wraps to a negative number.
- `left + (right - left) / 2` is the same midpoint, bounded and safe.
- Most relevant for **answer-space** binary search where bounds reach ~2 billion.
- **Zero performance cost** - same number of operations; use it by default.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: I use left plus the quantity right minus left divided by two instead of left plus right divided by two because the simpler version can overflow. In Java an int is a 32-bit signed value, so it maxes out around two point one billion. If left and right are both large, and that really happens when you binary search an answer space that can go up to about two billion rather than just a small array, then adding them together produces a sum bigger than the maximum an int can hold. The dangerous part is that Java doesn't throw an exception when this happens. It silently wraps around to a negative number, so your middle index becomes negative and the search either crashes with an out-of-bounds access or quietly returns the wrong answer. The safe formula avoids ever forming that oversized sum. Right minus left is just the size of the current range, which is always smaller than either endpoint, so it can't overflow. I halve that gap and add it back to left, and the result is exactly the same midpoint, just computed in a way that stays within bounds. What I'd emphasize in an interview is that this costs nothing. It's the same number of operations, so there's no reason not to write it the safe way every time. It signals that I think about edge cases and that I know integer overflow in Java is silent rather than something the runtime will catch for me. It's a one-line habit that prevents a rare but genuinely hard-to-debug failure in production code that handles large ranges.

questions.question: Can binary search be applied to problems other than searching in sorted arrays?
questions.title: Binary Search Applications Beyond Arrays
questions.direct_answer: Yes - binary search works on any **monotonic search space**, not just arrays. If you can write a **decision function** `feasible(x)` that is false up to some point and then true forever after (or vice versa), you can binary search for the boundary. This 'binary search on the answer' solves problems like minimum shipping capacity, Koko eating bananas, and integer square root in **O(log(range) x cost-of-check)**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you see binary search as a pattern over a monotonic predicate, not only an array operation
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Believing binary search needs a physical sorted array, so missing optimization problems that have no array
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Spot the 'minimum/maximum value that satisfies a condition' phrasing and map it to a feasible() predicate

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Binary search needs a **monotonic predicate**, not a literal sorted array.
- The search space is the **range of candidate answers** (`lo..hi`).
- `feasible(x)` replaces the array comparison; keep it **O(n)** or better.
- Total cost = **O(log(range) x cost-of-feasible)**.
- Trigger phrase: 'smallest/largest value such that ...'.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Yes, binary search is much more general than searching a sorted array. The real requirement is a monotonic search space, meaning I can write a decision function that's false for small candidate values and then flips to true at some threshold and stays true. The pattern of answers looks like false, false, false, true, true, true, and binary search just finds where it flips. A great example is Koko eating bananas. I'm asked for the minimum eating speed so that all the banana piles are finished within a given number of hours. There's no array to search here. The space is the range of possible speeds, from one up to the largest pile. For each candidate speed I write a feasibility check that adds up how many hours it would take at that speed, and returns true if it fits in the time limit. As speed increases, the hours needed only ever go down, so feasibility is monotonic, which is exactly what binary search needs. I start with a low and a high speed, take the midpoint, and if that speed is feasible I try something slower, otherwise I speed up. Another example is integer square root, where I binary search the answer from one to n and check whether mid times mid is too big. The mistake freshers make is assuming binary search needs a physical sorted array, so they miss these optimization problems entirely. My trigger is the phrasing: whenever a problem asks for the smallest or largest value that satisfies some condition, and I can check a candidate efficiently, I think binary search on the answer, which turns a linear scan over candidates into a logarithmic one.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Binary search the **answer space** from 1 to n.

For the integer square root: if `mid*mid == n` return `mid`; if `mid*mid < n` record `mid` and go right (`left = mid + 1`); else go left (`right = mid - 1`).

Return the last `mid` whose square was `<= n` (the **floor**). Cast `mid*mid` to `long` to avoid overflow. Time is **O(log n)**.

Computing mid as (left + right) / 2 (overflows for large indices) and updating boundaries to mid instead of mid +/- 1, causing infinite loops

sections.title: Answer-Space Binary Search
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB A[lo = min answer
hi = max answer] --> B{lo < hi?} B -- no --> Z[return lo
smallest feasible] B -- yes --> C[mid = lo + hi-lo/2] C --> D{feasible mid ?} D -- true --> E[hi = mid
try smaller] D -- false --> F[lo = mid + 1
need bigger] E --> B F --> B ```

sections.title: Koko Eating Bananas - Search the Speed
When This Pattern Applies
sections.content:
- The problem asks for a **minimum or maximum value that satisfies a condition** (capacity, speed, pages, days, length).
- You can write a **`feasible(x)`** check, usually O(n), that is **monotonic** - once true it stays true.
- Brute-forcing every candidate is too slow; binary search cuts the candidate range to O(log(range)).
- Examples beyond arrays: integer square root, rotated-array pivot, first bad version in a deployment history.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: **`Arrays.binarySearch()`** is Java's built-in binary search on a pre-sorted array: it returns the index if found, or the encoded value **`-(insertionPoint) - 1`** if not. A **manual binary search** is the loop you write yourself, which you need for variants the library can't do - first/last occurrence, rotated arrays, or binary search on an answer space. Both are O(log n); the difference is control versus convenience.

questions.question: How do you find the first and last occurrence of a number in a sorted array?
questions.title: First Last Occurrence Binary Search | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Run two boundary binary searches that **don't stop on the first match**. For the **first** position, on a match record the index and keep searching left (`right = mid - 1`). For the **last** position, record and keep searching right (`left = mid + 1`). Each is **O(log n)**, far better than finding one match and scanning, which is O(n) when the array is all duplicates.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can turn the standard template into a leftmost/rightmost search and keep it logarithmic
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Finding any match then linearly scanning outward, degrading to O(n) on heavy duplicates
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use a stored result variable and explain count = last - first + 1 in O(log n)

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Two boundary searches: **first** narrows left, **last** narrows right.
- Store the index on a match, then keep going - never return early.
- Each search is **O(log n)**; two of them is still O(log n).
- Occurrence count = `last - first + 1`.
- Initialize `ans = -1` for a missing target.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: To find the first and last position of a value in a sorted array I run two binary searches, and the key change in both is that I don't stop when I find a match. For the first position, I do a normal binary search, but when the middle element equals the target I save that index in a result variable and then move right down to mid minus one. That keeps me searching the left half, because any earlier copy of the target has to be on the left. I keep going until the range is empty, and the saved index is the leftmost occurrence. For the last position it's the mirror image: on a match I save the index and move left up to mid plus one, so I keep searching the right half for a later copy. Both searches stay O of log n because I'm still halving the range each step, I've just changed what I do on a match. The mistake I want to avoid is finding one match with binary search and then walking outward with a loop to find the edges. That looks fine, but if the array is all the same value, that linear walk is O of n and defeats the purpose. Using the stored result variable keeps everything logarithmic. A nice bonus is that once I have the first and last indices, the number of times the value appears is just last minus first plus one, computed in constant time. This is exactly LeetCode thirty-four, and it's a clean example of adapting the standard template to find boundaries instead of any single match.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
Binary search the **answer space** from 1 to n.

For the integer square root: if `mid*mid == n` return `mid`; if `mid*mid < n` record `mid` and go right (`left = mid + 1`); else go left (`right = mid - 1`).

Return the last `mid` whose square was `<= n` (the **floor**). Cast `mid*mid` to `long` to avoid overflow. Time is **O(log n)**.

Computing mid as (left + right) / 2 (overflows for large indices) and updating boundaries to mid instead of mid +/- 1, causing infinite loops

sections.title: Two Boundary Searches
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB S[target found?] --> A[findFirst:
on match go LEFT
right = mid - 1] S --> B[findLast:
on match go RIGHT
left = mid + 1] A --> C[first index] B --> D[last index] C --> E[count = last - first + 1] D --> E ```

Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Linear scan after a hit**: O(n) on `{2,2,...,2}` - the whole point is to avoid that.
- **Returning on first match**: yields an arbitrary copy, not the boundary.
- **Not storing `ans`**: moving boundaries without saving the index loses the match.
- **Off-by-one on count**: it's `last - first + 1`, not `last - first`.

sections.title: Important trade-off
sections.content: **`Arrays.binarySearch()`** is Java's built-in binary search on a pre-sorted array: it returns the index if found, or the encoded value **`-(insertionPoint) - 1`** if not. A **manual binary search** is the loop you write yourself, which you need for variants the library can't do - first/last occurrence, rotated arrays, or binary search on an answer space. Both are O(log n); the difference is control versus convenience.

questions.question: How do you search in a rotated sorted array?
questions.title: Search Rotated Sorted Array | Java Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: In a **rotated sorted array**, at every step **at least one half is normally sorted**. Compute `mid`, decide which half (left or right of `mid`) is sorted by comparing endpoints, then check whether the target lies inside that sorted half's range: if yes search it, otherwise search the other half. Each step still halves the array, so it's **O(log n)**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can spot and exploit the 'one half is always sorted' invariant instead of giving up on binary search
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reverting to an O(n) linear scan, or using strict < so the left == mid single-element case is misclassified
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: State the invariant explicitly and use nums[left] <= nums[mid] to detect the sorted half safely

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Invariant**: after `mid`, one half (`[lo..mid]` or `[mid..hi]`) is fully sorted.
- Detect the sorted half with `nums[lo] <= nums[mid]`.
- Search the sorted half only if the target lies in its range; else search the other half.
- **O(log n)** - rotation doesn't change the halving.
- Duplicates degrade the worst case to **O(n)**.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: Searching a rotated sorted array is a nice example of adapting binary search by spotting an invariant. A rotated array is just a sorted array that's been cut at some pivot and the two pieces swapped, like four five six seven zero one two. The invariant I rely on is that no matter where I compute the middle, at least one of the two halves, the part left of mid or the part right of mid, is still perfectly sorted. So at each step I first check if the middle is the target. If not, I figure out which half is sorted by comparing endpoints. If nums at low is less than or equal to nums at mid, the left half is sorted; otherwise the right half is. Once I know which half is sorted, I check whether the target's value falls inside that half's range. If it does, I search that half; if it doesn't, the target must be in the other half, the one that contains the rotation point, so I search there. Either way I throw away half the array, so I keep the O of log n time. Two details I'm careful about. I use less than or equal when comparing the low endpoint to mid, because with a strict less than the single-element case where low equals mid gets misclassified. And I always check that the target is actually between the sorted half's two endpoints, not just on one side of mid. The common mistake is panicking and reverting to a linear scan, but the rotation only creates one break, and identifying the sorted half lets binary search keep working. If the array can contain duplicates, I'd note the worst case can slip to O of n.

Return the last `mid` whose square was `<= n` (the **floor**). Cast `mid*mid` to `long` to avoid overflow. Time is **O(log n)**.

- **Skipping the range check**: you must verify the target is *within* the sorted half's endpoints, not just on one side of `mid`.
- **Duplicates**: equal values can break the endpoint comparison and push worst case to O(n) - mention it.

questions.question: How do you find the square root of a number using binary search?
questions.title: Square Root Binary Search Java | Fresher Interview
questions.direct_answer: Binary search the **answer space** from 1 to n. For the integer square root: if `mid*mid == n` return `mid`; if `mid*mid < n` record `mid` and go right (`left = mid + 1`); else go left (`right = mid - 1`). Return the last `mid` whose square was `<= n` (the **floor**). Cast `mid*mid` to `long` to avoid overflow. Time is **O(log n)**.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you recognize this as binary search on a monotonic answer space rather than reaching for Math.sqrt()
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling Math.sqrt() (defeats the question) or computing mid*mid as int and overflowing for large n
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Say explicitly 'I'm searching the answer space 1..n' and guard the multiplication with a long cast

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- This is **binary search on the answer space** `1..n`, no array involved.
- The predicate `mid*mid <= n` is **monotonic** - enables halving.
- Cast `mid*mid` to **`long`** to prevent overflow.
- Return the **floor**: last `mid` with `mid*mid <= n`.
- **O(log n)** time, **O(1)** space.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content: I'd solve this with binary search on the answer space from one to n, and I'd say that out loud, because the insight is that I'm not searching an array, I'm searching the range of possible answers. The possible square roots form a sorted sequence, and for any candidate I can decide whether it's too small, too big, or exactly right, which is all binary search needs. I set low to one and high to n. Each step I take the midpoint and compare mid times mid with n. If they're equal, mid is the exact square root and I return it. If mid times mid is less than n, then mid might be my answer, so I store it as a candidate and move low up to mid plus one to try larger values. If mid times mid is greater than n, mid is too big, so I move high down to mid minus one. When the loop ends, my stored candidate is the floor of the square root, the largest integer whose square doesn't exceed n. Two traps I'm careful about. First, I cast mid times mid to a long before comparing, because for large n that multiplication overflows a regular int and gives a wrong, even negative, result. Second, I return the stored candidate, not low, because when the loop exits low has gone one past the floor. The whole thing is O of log n time and constant space. And the bigger point I'd make is that this same answer-space technique solves a whole family of problems, anything where I'm optimizing a value and can check a candidate efficiently.

ans=0] --> B{lo <= hi?} B -- no --> Z[return ans

sq = long mid*mid] C --> D{sq vs n} D -- equal --> E[return mid] D -- sq < n --> F[ans = mid
lo = mid + 1] D -- sq > n --> G[hi = mid - 1] F --> B G --> B ```

- **Returning `lo` instead of `ans`**: at exit `lo` is one past the floor; return the stored `ans` (or `hi`).
- **Skipping `n < 2`**: 0 and 1 are their own square roots.
